newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANWEST SAYS TO ASSESS COURT RULING.
newsitem.headline: CANWEST SAYS TO ASSESS COURT RULING.

text.p: CanWest Global Communications Corp said on Friday it was examining the ruling by Australia's Federal Court that found in favour of the Australian Broadcasting Authority's (ABA) stance that CanWest had majority control of television network group TEN.

"We are assessing the decision with respect to the ABA," CanWest chairman Izzy Asper said in a statement issued in Australia. The ABA said CanWest has a 52.49 percent voting interest in TEN and a 76 percent economic interest.
Sources close to CanWest said the Canadian group only exercises voting control over 15 percent of TEN.
Justice Hill also ruled against Australian treasurer Peter Costello's decision that CanWest must reduce its economic interest to at least 57.5 percent.
"CanWest welcomes the rejection of the onerous orders imposed by the treasurer," Asper said.

"All we have sought is an orderly process, with a reasonable period of time, to implement a restructuring of Network TEN," he said. "We are, indeed, in intensive discussions with the authorities to achieve a mutually satisfactory conclusion."
"Today's decision helps advance that objective," he said.
In a separate statement, ABA chairman Peter Webb said he welcomed the ruling that dismissed applications for a review of its decision that CanWest was illegally in control of TEN.

CanWest increased its interest in the third-ranked Ten Network to 76 percent from 57.5 percent. The extra 18.5 percent holding was purchased by Donholken Pty Ltd and Selli Pty Ltd, with the acquisition debt financed by firms linked to CanWest.
The ABA, the statutory body which administers broadcasting laws and the government's industry adviser, has said CanWest must reduce its voting interest in TEN by October 3, 1997.
"The ABA welcomes the court's decision which vindicates its investigation process and findings," Webb said.

"The decision means that the ABA's orginal six month timetable remains undisturbed and continues to be due to expire in the first week of October. CanWest remains under an obligation to rectify the breach within this period," Webb said.

ABA said it examined share transactions which took place in November 1996 and January 1997. Shares in TEN, which were previously held by interests associated with John Singleton, Robert Whyte, Jack Cowin and others were sold to companies whose purchase was financed by CanWest.
ABA said these shares totalled 37.49 percent of the issued capital of TEN.

It said CanWest can apply for an extension of the period to remedy the breach. The ABA was not required to grant an extension, but if its does, the period of the extension cannot be more than six months.
It said there are significant penalties for the failure to comply with the Australian Broadcasting Act.
